items.title: Doping decides whether silicon's defects clump, and the curve is a U
items.dek: A three-author first-principles study screens more than 1,500 point-defect structures in silicon and finds that the Fermi level — the doping-set energy that fixes each defect's charge state — shifts the driving force for defects to bind into complexes by 0.3 to 0.5 electronvolts.
items.why_it_matters: Defect engineering in silicon is normally done with temperature and time: anneal hot enough and long enough and the complexes form or dissolve. Making the driving force a function of the Fermi level adds a knob the wafer already carries, because background doping sets where that level sits. Concentration is exponential in the enthalpy, so the 0.3 to 0.5 electronvolt span reported here works out to five to eight orders of magnitude in equilibrium complex concentration at room temperature — the difference between a species you can ignore and the dominant one.
items.background_md: Silicon crystals are never perfect. Vacancies, self-interstitials and light impurities such as carbon, oxygen, nitrogen and boron sit in the lattice and move during every hot process step, and what they do next matters electrically: a lone vacancy and a vacancy bound to an oxygen atom are different objects, one of which kills minority-carrier lifetime. Each defect also holds a charge state, and which state is lowest in energy depends on where the Fermi level sits, so the energy cost of any reaction between defects is a function of doping rather than a fixed constant.
items.deeper_md:
The screen was an unbiased global structure search with first-principles calculations over more than 1,500 candidate structures, covering intrinsic defects plus C, H, O, N, P and B impurities in charge states from −2 to +2.

The U shape is charge bookkeeping. A complex is generally closer to charge-neutral than the separate defects it was assembled from, so the aggregation reaction hands net charge back to the electron reservoir or takes some from it, and the enthalpy therefore carries a term proportional to that transferred charge multiplied by E_F. Where the net transfer passes through zero the linear term vanishes and binding is at its strongest; toward either band edge the term grows and binding weakens. The paper is explicit that the position of that zero is set by the charge transition levels of the particular defects involved, not by the middle of the gap.

Two caveats. The claim is thermodynamic — it is about equilibrium concentrations, not about whether a real anneal has time to reach them. And the charge-state dependence of a single defect's formation energy is textbook and undisputed; what is new is the non-monotonic shape of the *reaction* enthalpy, and that rests on computed transition levels, which is exactly the quantity different exchange-correlation functionals disagree about.

glossary.definition: The energy at which a state is equally likely to be filled or empty; doping moves it toward one band edge or the other, and its position decides which charge state a defect adopts.
The Fermi-level position at which a defect's lowest-energy charge state changes — for instance from neutral to singly negative — so it is where the defect begins or stops trapping a carrier.
The energy released when separate defects bind into one complex; more negative means binding is more favoured, and the equilibrium concentration of the complex depends on it exponentially.
The energy an electron gains falling through one volt. Silicon's band gap is about 1.12 eV, so a 0.4 eV shift moves the argument across a third of the gap.

items.fab_angle: Lifetime and gettering recipes are written as temperature and time. If the driving force also tracks E_F, then substrate resistivity is part of the recipe, which is worth knowing before a teaching lab runs one anneal on n-type and p-type wafers and compares the results.

sources.title: U-Shaped Fermi-Level Dependence of Point-Defect Aggregation Enthalpy in Silicon

First principles study of the T-center in Silicon

items.title: In hafnia, the boundary between two phases picks the winner
items.dek: A three-author atomistic simulation study of hafnium dioxide — the gate insulator in modern transistors, and the host of the metastable polar phase that ferroelectric memory depends on — finds that which crystal phase survives is decided at the boundary between two phases rather than by bulk free energy.
items.why_it_matters: Hafnia's ferroelectric phase is not the ground state; monoclinic is. Every recipe that yields a working ferroelectric capacitor is really a recipe for preventing the film from relaxing into monoclinic during crystallisation. If the deciding variable is which crystallographic planes happen to meet at a grain boundary, then grain orientation and texture become process handles with the same standing as dopant fraction and anneal temperature, and a film calculated to be phase-stable in the bulk can still convert along an interface the bulk calculation never contained.
items.background_md: Hafnium dioxide is polymorphic: one composition, several crystal structures. It can be monoclinic, tetragonal, or one of two orthorhombic forms, and only the polar orthorhombic one is ferroelectric — it holds a remanent polarisation that a voltage can flip and a later read can detect. Monoclinic is the lowest-energy structure at room temperature, so in a working device the useful phase is always the metastable one, held there by some combination of dopants, mechanical stress, film thickness and a capping layer that constrains the film while it crystallises.
items.deeper_md:
The simulations run a machine-learned interatomic potential with a hafnium-centred local phase classifier, so each Hf atom is labelled by the phase of its neighbourhood and phase fronts can be watched moving.

The results split by which two phases meet. The M(100)/T(100) interface stays pinned as a monoclinic/tetragonal mixture across 3 ns from 300 to 1800 K. M/PO, M/AO and PO/AO interfaces hold two-phase coexistence up to 900 K, while every T/PO interface goes polar-orthorhombic-dominant. At 1800 K all non-monoclinic interfaces become tetragonal-dominant, but anything containing monoclinic keeps a monoclinic majority.

The transformation barriers move too. Nudged elastic band calculations put the interface-mediated M(100)→T(100) route in a ~12 nm cell at 136.03 meV per formula unit, 29.2 % below the direct route in a ~3 nm cell, and attribute the gap to sequential phase-front motion that the short cell is too small to represent.

That attribution is also the caveat: a barrier that depends on cell length is partly a statement about the simulation box. Add that 3 ns is many orders of magnitude shorter than a crystallisation anneal, and that the potential is only as good as the density-functional data behind it. The field already disagrees about what stabilises the polar phase — stress versus lattice strain, dopants, surface energy, oxygen vacancies — and this adds interface orientation to that list rather than closing it.

glossary.definition: One of several crystal structures a single chemical composition can take. Hafnia's polymorphs sit close enough in energy that processing, not thermodynamics alone, decides which one a film ends up in.

The non-centrosymmetric hafnia structure in which part of the oxygen sublattice can be displaced by a field and stays displaced when the field is removed — the structural reason a hafnia capacitor is ferroelectric.
Millielectronvolts per formula unit: energy normalised to one HfO₂ unit so that simulation cells of different sizes can be compared directly.
A method that relaxes a chain of intermediate structures between two endpoints to find the lowest-energy path, and reports the height of its highest point as the activation barrier.

items.fab_angle: If the anneal's outcome depends on which grains touch which, texture control moves upstream into the deposition step: what the film looks like before crystallisation starts is part of the ferroelectric recipe, not a detail downstream of it.

sources.title: Interface-Controlled Phase Stability in Polymorphic HfO2 Revealed by Machine-Learning Atomistic Simulations
Disentangling stress and strain effects in ferroelectric HfO2
Epitaxial ferroelectric hafnia stabilized by symmetry constraints

items.title: Filling a via with magnet cancels an MRAM cell's built-in bias
items.dek: A four-author micromagnetic study proposes cancelling the built-in magnetic bias in a spin-orbit-torque MRAM cell — the asymmetry that makes one write direction cost more current than the other — by filling an adjacent back-end-of-line via with magnetic material instead of adding compensation layers inside the magnetic stack.
items.why_it_matters: Write-current asymmetry is paid twice: the driver transistor must be sized for the worse direction, and the array's write energy is set by that same worst case. Putting the compensating field in a neighbouring via rather than in the junction separates the two design problems, so the fix stops competing with the tunnel barrier, the reference layer and the pinning structure for thickness budget in a stack where every added layer is another deposition and another etch. The simulated compensation survives shrinking the junction to about 10 nm across.
items.background_md: A magnetic tunnel junction stores a bit as the relative orientation of two magnetic layers separated by a thin magnesium oxide barrier: one layer is pinned, the other is free to flip, and the resistance differs between parallel and antiparallel. The pinned layer is never magnetically silent. Its own stray field, plus exchange coupling through the barrier, leaves a small residual field on the free layer, tilting the energy landscape the free layer sits in. One switching direction is then downhill and the other uphill, so the two write currents are unequal by construction.
items.deeper_md:
The compensation is geometric. A via next to the junction, filled with magnetic material during back-end-of-line processing, produces its own stray field at the junction's location; choosing where the junction sits relative to that structure sets how much of the reference layer's field is cancelled. Optimising that placement takes the write-current bias ratio from 21.6 % in the conventional design to 1.3 % for the perpendicular case, and from 19.8 % to −0.2 % for an in-plane-anisotropy SOT junction. A scaling sweep keeps the effect at 20 % of the original device dimension, roughly a 10 nm junction diameter.

Note what the −0.2 % means: the compensation overshot and changed sign. The field is a function of a geometry that a real process holds only to its overlay and critical-dimension tolerances, so the interesting number is not 1.3 % but how fast the ratio degrades as the via drifts — which this work does not report.

The rest of the caveat is that these are micromagnetic simulations with no fabricated device, published in Acta Physica Sinica with the arXiv posting an English translation. The established alternative, an extra compensation layer inside the stack, is what shipped SOT-MRAM demonstrations have used; its cost is stack complexity, and that is precisely the trade being argued here.

glossary.definition: A torque on a magnet produced by charge current in an adjacent heavy-metal line, which converts part of that current into a transverse spin current; it writes the bit without driving current through the tunnel barrier.

The field the free layer feels with no current flowing, coming from the reference layer's stray field and from coupling through the barrier; it is what makes the two switching directions energetically unequal.
The fractional difference between the currents needed to switch a cell in its two directions. The study reports it falling from 21.6 % to 1.3 %.
The metal-filled hole joining one wiring level to the next above the transistors; here one is filled with magnetic material so that it works as a local field source rather than only as a conductor.

sources.title: Influence of magnetic fields on the performance of spin-orbit torque magnetic random-access memory
Offset fields in perpendicularly magnetized tunnel junctions
Spin-orbit torque switching of magnetic tunnel junctions for memory application
sources.publisher: arXiv / Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials

items.title: A KV cache laid out for the memory's math and the server's plumbing
items.dek: PATTON, a runtime from a four-author group, lets a production large-language-model server keep its key-value cache — the per-token memory a model rereads to produce each new token — inside commodity processing-in-memory DRAM, where the multiply happens on the memory chip instead of on the accelerator.
items.why_it_matters: Processing-in-memory demonstrations have mostly run attention over a static, preloaded matrix, which hides the part that breaks: a serving engine allocates, fills, shares, caches and reclaims cache blocks continuously, and the physical layout that makes the in-memory matrix-vector multiply fast is the same layout that makes writing one freshly generated token slow. Stating that as a three-way conflict between multiply efficiency, single-token write cost and capacity utilisation — and then resolving it in the allocator rather than in the memory hardware — is what moves this from a kernel benchmark toward something a serving stack could adopt.
items.background_md: Generating one token means multiplying stored weights and a stored cache by a single vector. That operation touches far more bytes than it does arithmetic, so on an accelerator it is limited by how fast memory can be read rather than by how fast the multipliers run. Processing-in-memory attacks this by placing small arithmetic units beside each DRAM bank, where the internal bandwidth is several times what the chip's external pins can carry. The price is that each unit can only see the rows of the bank it is attached to, so data placement becomes part of the algorithm.
items.deeper_md:
The conflict is concrete. A layout tuned for matrix-vector multiply spreads a vector across rows so the reduction runs in parallel — which means a newly generated Value vector has to be written into many scattered places. Sharing memory at a finer grain raises capacity utilisation but chops the reduction into fragments.

PATTON's answer is hierarchical granule allocation. Block-sized Key and Value granules map one-to-one onto the engine's logical token blocks, which fixes their physical placement and therefore the command sequence the runtime has to emit. Coarser granules group those blocks so a reduction still runs over contiguous storage. A Commit Zone stages partial Value blocks where single-token writes are cheap and commits them into the multiply-optimised locations once a block is full. The runtime tracks placements to generate the cache writes and the QK-transpose and SV commands itself.

Reported: 1.95× average speedup and 4.83× higher energy efficiency over the evaluated baselines across attention execution and runtime-induced prefill recomputation, with no change to the PIM processing units and a cache hit rate comparable to vLLM's native GPU cache.

Caveat: those are averages over a baseline set the abstract does not enumerate, and it does not say whether the numbers come from silicon or a simulator. "Commodity PIM" means the design targets parts that exist; an end-to-end serving measurement on a shipping PIM module is not claimed. The standing criticism of PIM is that the win disappears once host-side bookkeeping is counted, and measuring that bookkeeping is exactly what this work sets out to do.

glossary.definition: The keys and values a transformer already computed for every earlier token, kept so each new token can attend to them without recomputation; it grows with sequence length and dominates memory during serving.
General matrix-vector multiply. It reads every matrix element once and does about two arithmetic operations per element, so its speed is set by memory bandwidth on essentially any processor.
DRAM with arithmetic units placed next to the banks so operands are multiplied where they are stored, exploiting internal bank bandwidth that is far larger than the chip's external pin bandwidth.
Here, the unit of physical DRAM the runtime allocates in one go. Keys and values are given different granule sizes because they are written and read in different patterns.

sources.title: PATTON: Enabling Commodity PIM for Production LLM Serving
Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention

items.title: Two GPU kernels that agree on the math and not on the bits
items.dek: A four-author team reconstructed the arithmetic hidden inside NVIDIA's closed-source cuBLAS library well enough for their own matrix-multiply kernels to match it bit for bit on Blackwell and Hopper, then built a static checker that decides whether two compiled GPU kernels add their partial sums in the same order.
items.why_it_matters: Floating-point addition is not associative, so a matrix multiply's exact answer depends on the order its partial sums are combined — and that order is chosen by whichever tile shape an autotuner found fastest for the batch size in front of it. The practical consequence is that the same prompt, the same weights and the same model can produce different tokens depending on how many other requests happened to be in flight. Turning bit equivalence into a property a checker can decide on compiled code lets the autotuner keep searching for speed inside one equivalence class instead of trading reproducibility away for it.
items.background_md: A floating-point number carries a fixed number of significant bits, so adding a large value to a small one discards part of the small one. Addition therefore is not associative: (a+b)+c and a+(b+c) can differ in the last bits. A matrix multiply is a long sum of products, and a GPU splits that sum across thousands of threads and several levels of hardware. How many pieces the sum is cut into, in what order they are recombined, at what intermediate precision, and where the rounding happens are all implementation choices rather than properties of the operation being computed.
items.deeper_md:
The paper's first move is a descriptor for a GEMM's reduction order, including how the summed dimension K is partitioned in split-K. With that descriptor they carry out what they describe as the first black-box reconstruction of a closed-source library's arithmetic: their family of Triton GEMMs matches cuBLAS in every tested case on Blackwell and Hopper, and on realistic LLM shapes with fused epilogues it matches or beats torch.compile.

Holding an order fixed is not free — they put the cost at up to 20 percent. So they enforce balanced-tree reduction during Triton lowering and add a data-layout optimisation that brings 19 of 27 kernels on GB300 and H100 within 10 percent of free-order performance. The third piece is a sound static checker for bitwise equivalence between compiled kernels, the first to span NVIDIA PTX and AMD GCN, wired into Triton's autotuner so its search is confined to a single bit-equivalence class.

Caveats worth holding. Eight of the 27 kernels are still outside 10 percent and the abstract does not say by how much. "Sound" means the checker never certifies equivalence that does not hold; it says nothing about how often it has to answer that it cannot tell. Nobody disputes the mechanism — PyTorch's own reproducibility notes state plainly that each backend accumulates in a different order and that results will therefore differ between backends. The argument is over whether that is a documented limitation or a bug worth paying 20 percent to remove.

glossary.definition: The property that floating-point (a+b)+c need not equal a+(b+c), because every addition rounds to a fixed number of bits; it is why the value of a long sum depends on the order it is accumulated.
General matrix-matrix multiply, the operation most of a transformer's arithmetic reduces to. Libraries implement it by cutting the matrices into tiles and combining partial sums across them.

A GEMM strategy that divides the summed dimension among separate thread blocks and adds their results afterwards, which inserts one more level into the reduction tree and one more way for the bits to diverge.
The property that one element's result does not change when unrelated elements are batched alongside it. A kernel that picks a different tile shape per batch size does not have it.

sources.title: Taming Bitwise Behavior in GPU Kernels with Tensor Core: Black-Box Reconstruction, Compiler Enforcement, and Static Verification
Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference
Reproducibility — PyTorch notes on nondeterministic algorithms

items.title: Sparse models run out of fresh text sooner than dense ones
items.dek: A five-author study reports that mixture-of-experts language models — which route each token to a few of many parallel sub-networks instead of running all of them — begin to lose ground to repeated training data at four passes over the same corpus, where dense models of the same parameter count tolerate eight.
items.why_it_matters: Every scaling plan for sparse models rests on adding experts to buy parameters without buying arithmetic. If the tolerance for repetition falls as sparsity rises, then how many parameters a sparse model can usefully carry is bounded by how much unique text exists rather than by the training budget, and those two limits have to be planned against separately. The authors name expert specialisation and routing stability as the mechanisms, which matters because it says the problem is not fixed by training for fewer steps: a specialised expert sees a narrower slice of the corpus than the model as a whole does.
items.background_md: A dense transformer runs every parameter on every token. A mixture-of-experts layer instead holds many parallel feed-forward blocks plus a router that sends each token to a small subset of them, so the parameter count grows while the arithmetic per token does not. The cost is that each expert only ever trains on the tokens routed to it, and the router's choices keep moving while training proceeds. Separately, the supply of human-written text is finite, so large training runs now make several passes over the same corpus instead of always consuming fresh tokens.
items.deeper_md:
The comparison is held at equal parameter count. Dense 80M-parameter models absorb 8× repetition with little measurable loss; mixture-of-experts models at the same scale start degrading at 4×, and the effect strengthens as sparsity increases. That halving is the result: the usable repetition budget is a property of the architecture, not only of how much data you have.

The authors test mitigations. Dropout and masking-based regularisation help; none of them recovers the performance of training on all-unique data.

Two things to keep in view. First, the numbers sit in tension with the standard reference on data-constrained scaling, which put the dense knee at roughly 4 epochs — at far larger scale and under a different compute-optimal setup — so the absolute thresholds are not directly comparable and the paper's claim is really about the dense-versus-sparse gap rather than about either number alone. Second, 80M parameters is small, and repetition effects are known to interact with scale, so whether an 8-versus-4 gap survives at production sizes is precisely the extrapolation this evidence cannot make. The mechanism attribution — expert specialisation and routing stability — is an interpretation of observed behaviour rather than a controlled intervention, and it is the part most open to argument.

glossary.definition: A layer holding many parallel feed-forward blocks with a router that sends each token to a small subset, so total parameters rise without a matching rise in arithmetic per token.
Here, the share of a model's parameters left inactive on any given token. A model with 64 experts that activates 2 of them is sparser than one activating 8.
One complete pass over the training corpus. Repeating data means running several epochs, now standard practice because the stock of unique high-quality text is limited.
How consistently the router keeps sending similar tokens to the same expert as training proceeds. Unstable routing means an expert's effective training set changes underneath it.

sources.title: Data Scarcity and Model Sparsity: Mixtures-of-Experts Overfit More to Repeated Data
Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
Scaling Laws for Fine-Grained Mixture of Experts

foundations.topic: CVD: LPCVD, PECVD, and the pressure trade
foundations.subtitle: Why dropping the pressure to a fifth of a torr lets you grow the same film on fifty wafers at once, and why a plasma is how you deposit on something that must not get hot.
foundations.tldr: Chemical vapour deposition grows a film by flowing gases over a hot wafer and letting them react on its surface. Drop the pressure to a couple of hundred millitorr and the surface chemistry, not the gas supply, becomes the slow step — which means every wafer in the tube grows at the same rate, so you can stand fifty of them on edge in one furnace. Swap the heat for a plasma and you get similar films at 300 °C instead of 800 °C, paying for it in hydrogen trapped in the film and a stress you now have to tune deliberately.

sections.heading: Two slow steps, and you get to choose which one
sections.body_md:
A CVD film grows in a sequence: reactant gas has to reach the wafer, adsorb, react, and let the by-products leave. Two of those steps can be the bottleneck, and which one it is decides everything about the reactor.

At atmospheric pressure, molecules collide constantly and a stagnant boundary layer sits over the wafer. Getting fresh reactant through that layer is slow, so the growth rate is set by gas transport — by flow, by geometry, by where on the wafer you are. The chemistry is fast enough not to matter. This is the mass-transport-limited regime, and it forces a reactor where every wafer is presented to the flow individually.

Drop the pressure and the picture inverts. Gas-phase diffusivity rises roughly as one over pressure, so at a couple of hundred millitorr — against an atmosphere's 760 torr, nearly four orders of magnitude down — transport stops being the constraint. Now the surface reaction is slowest, and the growth rate follows an Arrhenius dependence on temperature and almost nothing else.
sections.deeper_md: The practical consequence is a swap of which variable you must control tightly. In the mass-transport regime, rate is weakly temperature-dependent and strongly dependent on flow uniformity, so you buy a single-wafer chamber with a carefully engineered showerhead. In the surface-reaction regime, rate is exponential in temperature and nearly indifferent to flow, so you buy a furnace that can hold a temperature to within a degree over a metre of tube — and you get to put a lot of wafers in that metre.

sections.heading: Why that lets you stand fifty wafers on edge
sections.body_md:
If growth rate depends only on the local temperature and the local reactant partial pressure, and neither varies much, then two wafers 5 mm apart grow the same film — even though the second one is nowhere near the gas inlet. That is the entire economic argument for low-pressure CVD, and you can read it straight off a university nanofab's tool list. DTU Nanolab's polysilicon furnaces take 1–50 wafers at 150–250 mTorr; its 150 mm nitride furnace takes up to 25 wafers at 150 mTorr.

The problem that survives is depletion. Gas entering one end of the tube is consumed as it travels, so the last wafers in the boat see a leaner mixture than the first. Because rate is exponential in temperature, a small deliberate temperature rise down the tube can offset a real drop in concentration, which is why a production LPCVD tube is heated in several independently controlled zones rather than one. Uniformity in LPCVD is a control problem, not a plumbing problem.
sections.deeper_md: Note that the same physics makes LPCVD conformal. In the surface-reaction-limited regime the arriving species do not stick where they first land; they have time to migrate and react wherever the surface offers a site. A trench sidewall is therefore coated at nearly the same rate as the flat top. That property is why LPCVD nitride and LPCVD oxide are what you reach for when a film has to coat topography — and it is also why the same films deposited in a transport-dominated regime pinch off narrow features instead of filling them.

sections.heading: Silane in, polysilicon out — and 40 °C decides the microstructure
sections.body_md:
The chemistry is unglamorous. Polysilicon comes from silane decomposing on a hot surface; DTU's recipe is 80 sccm of SiH₄ at 620 °C and 200–250 mTorr. Doping happens in the same step, with 7 sccm of diborane or phosphine added to the flow, so the film arrives already conductive rather than needing an implant.

The interesting number is 620 versus 560–580 °C. Same gas, same tool, same pressure, a difference of forty to sixty degrees — and the film comes out amorphous instead of polycrystalline. The reason is surface mobility: at 620 °C an arriving silicon atom has time to find a lattice site before the next layer buries it, and at 570 °C it does not. Amorphous silicon deposited cold and then crystallised in a separate anneal ends up with larger, more uniform grains than silicon that crystallised as it grew, which matters if the film is a MEMS structural layer whose stress depends on grain structure.
sections.deeper_md: The same temperature knob shows up in nitride through composition rather than crystallinity. DTU's stoichiometric Si₃N₄ recipe runs 20 sccm dichlorosilane against 80 sccm ammonia at 780–790 °C and 200 mTorr; its low-stress recipe inverts the ratio to 200 sccm dichlorosilane against 50 sccm ammonia at 810–845 °C and 150 mTorr. The low-stress film is deliberately silicon-rich. Stoichiometric LPCVD nitride is under high tensile stress and cracks above a few hundred nanometres; pushing excess silicon into the network relieves it, at the cost of a higher refractive index and a film that is no longer the same etch-stop it was.

sections.heading: When the wafer cannot get hot: plasma instead of temperature
sections.body_md:
LPCVD's temperatures are a hard constraint, not a preference. Kiel's electronic-materials hyperscript gives the two standard oxide reactions as dichlorosilane with nitrous oxide at 900 °C, and the TEOS route at 720 °C. Both are far above what aluminium interconnect tolerates, so neither can be used once metal is on the wafer. Anything deposited after metallisation has to find its energy somewhere other than the lattice.

A plasma is that somewhere. Apply radio-frequency power to a low-pressure gas and free electrons — light enough to be accelerated hard by the field — gain enough energy to break precursor molecules apart in the gas phase. The fragments arrive at the surface already reactive, so the wafer only has to be warm enough for them to stick and rearrange. Kiel puts the resulting process temperature at a few hundred degrees; Oxford Instruments' PECVD platform lists resistively heated electrodes up to 400 °C, and Caltech's KNI runs its equivalent tool from room temperature to 600 °C.
sections.deeper_md: This is the general shape of every plasma process step, not a fact about PECVD alone. A plasma is deeply out of equilibrium: the electrons are hot and the gas and the wafer are not, because the electrons are thousands of times lighter and exchange energy with the heavy particles poorly. That decoupling is what buys the chemistry without the temperature — and it is the same decoupling that makes reactive ion etching directional and sputtering possible. The cost is always the same too: you have now introduced energetic ion bombardment as an independent variable, and it will show up in the film whether you wanted it or not.

sections.heading: The bill for going cold: hydrogen, and a stress you must tune
sections.body_md:
PECVD precursors are hydrogen-bearing — silane, ammonia — and 300 °C is nowhere near hot enough to drive hydrogen back out of the growing film. So PECVD nitride is not Si₃N₄; it is SiN\_xH\_y, with Si–H and N–H bonds distributed through it. The consequences are practical: lower density, a faster etch rate in hydrofluoric acid than the LPCVD film, and outgassing if anything later heats the stack.

Stress is the other bill, and it is also the knob. Oxford Instruments' systems apply dual-frequency power to the upper electrode, 13.56 MHz and 100 kHz, and state plainly that film stress is controlled by mixing the two; Caltech's tool pairs a 30/300 W radio-frequency generator with a 600 W low-frequency generator running 50–460 kHz. The mechanism is ion inertia. At 13.56 MHz the field reverses faster than a heavy ion can respond, so ions drift in and land gently. At 100 kHz they follow the field, pick up energy, and hammer the growing film — compacting it and driving the stress compressive. The ratio of the two powers is a continuous dial between tensile and compressive.
sections.deeper_md: This is why a released MEMS membrane is usually specified by its stress rather than its material. A film left in compression buckles when you etch the sacrificial layer out from under it; a film in high tension cracks or tears at anchors. The target is typically slightly tensile — tens of megapascals — which is achievable in PECVD nitride by frequency mixing and in LPCVD nitride only by going silicon-rich. Measuring it is a wafer-curvature measurement: deposit on one side, measure the bow before and after, and apply Stoney's equation.

sections.heading: Choosing between them
sections.body_md:
The decision is nearly always thermal budget against film quality, and it is usually made for you by where in the flow the step sits.

Before metal, use LPCVD. It gives a denser, more conformal, better-controlled film, it coats topography almost evenly because the surface reaction is the slow step, and the 600–850 °C it demands is affordable when there is nothing above the transistors yet but polysilicon and dielectric. This is the regime for gate dielectrics, oxidation masks, etch stops, sacrificial layers and MEMS structural films.

After metal, use PECVD, because you have no choice. Accept the hydrogen, accept that the film grows faster where the flux is highest and can therefore close the mouth of a narrow trench before filling it, and spend your effort on the frequency mix that lands the stress where you want it. Passivation layers, inter-metal dielectric and post-processing encapsulation are all PECVD for exactly this reason — not because it is the better film, but because it is the only one the wafer can survive.
sections.deeper_md: There is a third option this framing leaves out, and it is worth knowing the name of: atomic layer deposition, which separates the reaction into two self-limiting half-reactions run alternately, so exactly one monolayer forms per cycle regardless of transport. ALD is perfectly conformal and runs at PECVD-like temperatures, which sounds like it dominates both — until you notice the rate. ALD deposits roughly an ångström per cycle at a cycle time of seconds, so a 100 nm film is a very long run. It won the gate dielectric and the high-aspect-ratio liner; it did not win the 500 nm passivation layer, and it is not going to.

glossary.definition: Chemical vapour deposition at a few hundred millitorr in a hot-wall tube furnace. Reduced pressure raises gas diffusivity enough that the surface reaction becomes the rate-limiting step, which makes growth uniform across a stack of wafers.

Chemical vapour deposition in which a radio-frequency plasma dissociates the precursors, so the wafer supplies only enough heat for the fragments to stick and rearrange. It deposits oxide and nitride at a few hundred degrees rather than 700–900 °C.

The regime in which the chemistry on the wafer is the slow step, so growth rate follows an Arrhenius dependence on temperature and is nearly independent of how gas flows past. It is what makes LPCVD both batchable and conformal.
The regime in which delivering reactant through the boundary layer is the slow step, so growth rate depends on the flow field and on position. Reactors operating here process wafers one at a time.

Standard cubic centimetres per minute — gas flow quoted as the volume it would occupy at a reference temperature and pressure, so a number like 200 sccm means a fixed number of molecules per minute whatever the chamber pressure happens to be.

How faithfully a deposited film follows topography. A perfectly conformal film is as thick on a trench sidewall as on the flat above it, which requires arriving species to migrate on the surface before they react.
The silicon precursor used with ammonia to grow LPCVD silicon nitride. The dichlorosilane-to-ammonia flow ratio sets how silicon-rich the film is, and therefore its stress and refractive index.

The cumulative time-at-temperature a wafer can absorb before already-built structures degrade. Metallisation is the step that collapses it, which is why everything deposited afterwards is a plasma process.

foundations.try_this: MNF's tube furnace is an LPCVD chassis minus the vacuum, so do the arithmetic that says why the vacuum is the point. Using the kinetic-theory mean free path λ = kT / (√2 π d² P) with a molecular diameter of about 0.5 nm, compute λ for silane at DTU's polysilicon pressure of 250 mTorr and again at one atmosphere, then compare each against the ~5 mm gap between wafers in a vertical boat. One answer says a molecule crosses the gap without hitting anything; the other says it has to diffuse through a crowd. Then read Van Zant, *Microchip Fabrication* 6e, ch. 12 on CVD, and check which reactor geometries the chapter assigns to each case.
